drills.q: What Richardson Maturity level does correct HTTP verb and status code usage correspond to?
Which RFC currently defines the Problem Details error contract, and which RFC did it supersede?
What HTTP header enables SSE's built-in reconnection to resume a stream rather than replay it from scratch?
A 'load more' feature gets measurably slower every week as a customer's order history grows. Diagnose and name the fix.
drills.a: Offset-based pagination -- the database scans and discards a growing number of rows on every deep page as the dataset grows. Fix: migrate to cursor-based pagination on an indexed sort column, which stays roughly constant-time regardless of depth into the dataset.

drills.q: A public API introduces v2 via a header (Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json) at the same URL as v1, and some clients intermittently receive v1 responses when requesting v2. Diagnose.
drills.a: The CDN or intermediate cache is keying purely on URL, not on the version header, because Vary: Accept (or equivalent) isn't correctly configured at every layer in the caching chain -- a cached v1 response gets served to a v2 request hitting the identical URL. URL-path versioning avoids this bug class entirely by construction.

drills.q: A team wants to build a live order-tracking feature and defaults to WebSocket 'to be safe for real-time.' Is this justified? What should they check first?
drills.a: Not necessarily justified -- check whether the feature is genuinely bidirectional. Order status push (server to client only) is squarely SSE's use case: built-in reconnection, CDN-transparent, less complexity. WebSocket is justified only if the client genuinely needs to push data back through the same low-latency channel, which most 'real-time' features don't actually require.

drills.q: Why do most production REST APIs deliberately stop at Richardson Maturity Level 2 rather than pursuing Level 3 (HATEOAS)?
drills.a: Level 3's benefit -- clients dynamically discovering available actions via response links instead of hardcoding URLs -- rarely pays off for the typical client population of a documented API, since engineers writing integration code are going to hardcode URL patterns regardless of whether a link is offered. The real, ongoing cost of correctly computing state-and-permission-aware links for every response usually isn't justified.

drills.q: Design the pagination and error-handling approach for a GraphQL layer aggregating three internal gRPC services for both a mobile and web client, and explain what happens if one of the three services degrades.
drills.a: Pagination: Relay-style cursor connections (edges/node/cursor/pageInfo), translating to cursor-based pagination in the underlying gRPC services for the same DB-performance reasons. Errors: map gRPC status/messages into GraphQL's errors array with structured extensions, giving both clients one consistent shape regardless of which internal service failed. On a degraded service: GraphQL returns a PARTIAL response -- successfully-resolved fields from healthy services plus a structured error entry for the degraded service's specific fields, rather than failing the whole query, unlike a typical REST aggregation endpoint which more commonly fails atomically.

drills.q: A partner integration reports both slow 'load more' performance and intermittent stale-data issues on a public API using offset pagination and header-based versioning. Diagnose both, and explain which fix requires partner-side changes and which doesn't.
drills.a: Slow load-more: offset-pagination performance cliff, worsening as the partner's dataset grows -- migrate to cursor pagination, which can be introduced as an ADDITIVE, backward-compatible change alongside the existing offset parameters, not requiring immediate partner-side changes. Stale data: likely a Vary-header misconfiguration in the caching chain for header-based versioning, serving a cached response from the wrong version -- fixable entirely server-side by correcting the Vary configuration, again with no client-side change required.

drills.q: Why is tRPC the wrong choice for a public API with external partner consumers, even though it eliminates contract-drift bugs for internal use?
drills.a: tRPC's value proposition depends on both ends sharing TypeScript types directly (same monorepo or a shared type-generation pipeline) -- an external partner's codebase, likely in a different language or an entirely separate repo, can't consume that shared-type mechanism at all. REST (or GraphQL for diverse-shape needs) remains correct for any API surface with consumers outside your own TypeScript codebase.

drills.q: Where do idempotency keys belong architecturally -- API design or the resilience/retry layer -- and why does that classification matter for how you design an endpoint?
drills.a: Both, in different roles: the endpoint's documented contract (accepting an Idempotency-Key header, defining behavior on a repeated key) is an API DESIGN concern, since it's client-visible and must be documented; the actual mechanism preventing double-processing (a dedup store, an atomic INSERT ON CONFLICT) is resilience-layer implementation (T21-resilience-catalogue). Designing an endpoint without documenting idempotency-key behavior leaves clients unable to safely retry costly mutations like payments -- a genuine API design gap, not just a missing retry policy.
